prompt: Which three elements together define an Azure RBAC role assignment?
choices: A security principal, a role definition, and a scope
A security principal, a Conditional Access policy, and a scope
A management group, a subscription, and a resource group
A role definition, a service tag, and a resource lock
correctAnswers: A security principal, a role definition, and a scope
explanation: A role assignment is who, what and where: a security principal, a role definition and a scope. A Conditional Access policy is the tempting fourth element because it also gates access, whereas it governs the sign-in rather than the permission and is not part of the assignment at all.

prompt: A user needs to create and manage all resources in a resource group but must NOT be able to grant other people access to those resources. Which built-in role is the least-privilege fit?
choices: Contributor on the group
User Access Administrator
Owner of the group
Reader on the group
explanation: Contributor manages resources but cannot create role assignments. Owner could also do it but additionally grants access (more than required); User Access Administrator only manages access, not resources.

prompt: Which built-in role can assign roles to other principals but grants no permission to create, modify, or delete the resources themselves?
choices: User Access Administrator
Managed Identity Operator role
Contributor on the scope
Owner of the whole scope
explanation: User Access Administrator manages access (role assignments) only. Owner can do both; Contributor manages resources but not access; Managed Identity Operator only manages managed-identity usage.

prompt: An Azure role is assigned at the subscription scope. Which statement about its effect is correct?
choices: It is inherited by every group and resource below
It applies only to resources that existed at assignment time
It must be re-created on each resource group to take effect
It only applies to the management group above it
correctAnswers: It is inherited by every group and resource below
explanation: RBAC permissions inherit downward, including to resources created later. Inheritance never flows upward to a management group.

prompt: In a custom Azure role definition, control-plane operations that are granted are listed under which property?
choices: The Actions array
The AssignableScopes array
The DataActions array
The NotActions array
explanation: Actions grants control-plane operations and NotActions subtracts from them. DataActions is the closest miss and operates on the data plane instead — the distinction decides whether a role can list a storage account or read the blobs inside it.

prompt: You are authoring a custom Azure role that must allow reading blob content but must NOT allow reconfiguring the storage account's network rules. In which property do the blob-read permissions belong?
choices: The DataActions array
The AssignableScopes array
The NotActions array
The Actions array
explanation: Reading blob content is a data-plane operation, so it belongs in DataActions. Actions is the tempting choice because it is the property most people know, however it would grant management of the account whereas the content would still be unreadable.

prompt: Which property of a custom Azure role definition limits the scopes at which the role can be assigned?
choices: The AssignableScopes array
The NotDataActions array list
The DataActions array list
The Condition property
explanation: AssignableScopes lists the management groups, subscriptions, or resource groups where the role may be assigned. It neither grants nor denies any permission.

prompt: Which statement best separates Azure roles from Microsoft Entra roles?
choices: Azure roles cover resources; Entra roles the directory
Azure roles control the directory; Entra roles control resources
They are the same permission system under two names
Only Entra roles support custom definitions
correctAnswers: Azure roles cover resources; Entra roles the directory
explanation: Azure roles control Azure resources; Entra roles control the directory. They are independent systems — both support custom roles, and neither grants anything in the other, which is why "same system, two names" is the belief to discard.

prompt: A Global Administrator reports they cannot see any subscription in the Azure portal. Which fact explains this best?
choices: Entra roles grant no Azure resource access
Subscriptions stay hidden until Conditional Access allows them
Global Administrator is a read-only Azure RBAC role
Microsoft support must add them to the tenant root
correctAnswers: Entra roles grant no Azure resource access
explanation: Entra roles do not grant access to Azure resources, so a Global Administrator holds nothing in a subscription by default. Assuming the directory role implies resource access is the confusion, whereas the elevation toggle exists precisely because it does not.

prompt: When a Global Administrator sets the 'Access management for Azure resources' toggle to Yes, what exactly happens?
choices: That user gets User Access Administrator at root
The tenant permanently switches every vault and account to RBAC
The user gets Contributor on the hierarchy for a day
Every Global Administrator gets Owner everywhere
correctAnswers: That user gets User Access Administrator at root
explanation: The toggle is a per-user elevation that assigns User Access Administrator at the tenant root scope. It does not grant Owner to every Global Administrator, which is the exaggerated reading — one user gains one assignment at one scope, and it should be removed afterwards.

prompt: In Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management, what does an 'eligible' assignment mean?
choices: The role must be activated before it is usable
The principal permanently holds it, with no activation needed
The principal is blocked from ever activating the role
The role is assigned but scoped to read-only actions
correctAnswers: The role must be activated before it is usable
explanation: Eligible means the role must be activated before it can be used, subject to whatever gates the policy sets. Permanently holding the role with no activation is the contrasting state — active — whereas eligibility is the whole basis on which PIM removes standing access.

prompt: Which requirement is NOT something a PIM role setting can enforce at activation time?
choices: That the resource sit in a given region
Approval by a designated named approver
Multifactor authentication at activation
A written justification for the request
correctAnswers: That the resource sit in a given region
explanation: PIM activation settings cover MFA, approval, justification, ticket info, and maximum duration — not resource geography, which is a Policy/region concern.

prompt: Which scenario is the primary use case for Privileged Identity Management?
choices: No standing access; elevate just in time
Applications authenticate to Key Vault without a stored secret
Traffic to a storage account is restricted to one subnet
Sensitive database columns are hidden from admins
correctAnswers: No standing access; elevate just in time
explanation: PIM exists so administrators hold no standing privileged access and elevate just in time, time-bound and gated. The other options describe managed identity, storage firewalls and Always Encrypted — all tempting because they are also least-privilege ideas, whereas none of them is about elevation.

prompt: To require MFA specifically for the Azure Resource Manager control plane (portal, Azure PowerShell, Azure CLI), which Conditional Access target resource do you select?
choices: Windows Azure Service Management API
Office 365 Exchange Online cloud resource
Microsoft Intune Enrollment app
Microsoft Graph resource app
explanation: The Resource Manager control plane is targeted through the Windows Azure Service Management API resource. Microsoft Graph is the tempting pick because it is the modern API everyone names, however it covers directory calls rather than ARM.

prompt: You created a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for Azure management and want to see its impact before enforcing it. Which setting should you use?
choices: The Report-only mode
Enabled for a named location
On, and fully enforced
Off, and not evaluated
explanation: Report-only evaluates the policy and logs what would have happened without enforcing it, which is how you avoid locking yourself out. Turning it On is the tempting shortcut, whereas a mistake in the assignment then locks out every administrator at once.

prompt: Why should emergency-access ('break-glass') accounts be excluded from a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA?
choices: So a policy error cannot lock out every admin
Because break-glass accounts are incapable of performing MFA
Because break-glass accounts must use legacy authentication
Because Conditional Access cannot evaluate cloud-only accounts
correctAnswers: So a policy error cannot lock out every admin
explanation: Break-glass accounts are the recovery path of last resort; excluding them prevents a total lockout if a policy or the MFA service fails.

prompt: A daemon service principal is not being blocked by your user-targeted Conditional Access MFA policy. Why, and what is the correct control?
choices: User-targeted policies skip service principals
You must convert the service principal into a managed identity first
The service principal must join the break-glass exclusion list
Conditional Access never applies to the management plane
explanation: Policies scoped to users/groups don't cover non-interactive service principals. Conditional Access for workload identities is the dedicated mechanism for them.

prompt: Where in the portal do you begin adding an Azure role assignment for a specific resource group?
choices: The group's Access control (IAM) blade
Microsoft Entra ID ▸ Roles and administrators
Microsoft Entra ID ▸ Enterprise applications
Subscription ▸ Resource providers blade
explanation: Azure role assignments are made on the resource, resource group or subscription Access control blade. Entra ID ▸ Roles and administrators is the closest miss and manages directory roles instead — the same word "role" for a different system.

prompt: Which tool on the Access control (IAM) blade lets you confirm the effective permissions a specific user has at a given scope?
choices: The Check access tool
Role assignments export
The diagnostic settings
The resource activity log
explanation: Check access reports the effective access a principal has at that scope, accounting for inherited assignments. The activity log is the tempting alternative because it also concerns who did what, whereas it records past operations rather than current permissions.

prompt: A user was granted Reader at a subscription and Owner on one resource group inside it. What is their effective access on that resource group?
choices: Owner — assignments are additive
Reader — the higher-scope assignment always wins
No access — the conflicting assignments cancel out
Contributor — Azure averages the two roles
explanation: The user keeps Reader everywhere and gains Owner on that resource group, because Azure RBAC is additive rather than hierarchical. Believing the higher-scope assignment wins is the misconception, and it is how excess privilege goes unnoticed: nothing is ever subtracted by a second assignment.

prompt: Which of these role types is used to manage app registrations and other directory objects, rather than Azure resources?
choices: A Microsoft Entra directory role
An Azure RBAC role, such as Contributor
A Key Vault access policy entry
A resource-group level lock
explanation: Managing app registrations and enterprise applications is a directory task, so it needs a Microsoft Entra role. An Azure RBAC role such as Contributor is the tempting answer, however it grants nothing in the directory no matter how broad its scope.

prompt: Why is assigning roles to Microsoft Entra groups generally preferred over assigning them to individual users?
choices: Access follows group membership automatically
Group assignments bypass any role definition
User assignments are unsupported at subscription scope
Only group assignments can be time-bound in PIM
explanation: Assigning to groups means access follows membership, so joining and leaving handles onboarding and offboarding. It does not bypass role definitions, which is the over-reading — the definition still decides what the group members can do.

prompt: Which capability lets you subtract specific permissions so that even an Owner cannot perform them at a scope?
choices: A deny assignment on the scope
A NotActions entry in the Owner role
A Reader role layered on top
A ReadOnly resource lock
correctAnswers: A deny assignment on the scope
explanation: Deny assignments explicitly block actions and take precedence over allow assignments, even for Owner. NotActions only shapes a custom role's own grants; a ReadOnly lock blocks writes/deletes but is not an RBAC deny and behaves differently.

prompt: You need to grant a principal permission to only start and restart a specific VM — nothing else. What is the correct least-privilege approach?
choices: A custom role with just those VM actions
Assign Owner at the resource group and add a resource lock
Add the principal to the Global Administrator Entra role
Assign the built-in Contributor role at the VM scope
correctAnswers: A custom role with just those VM actions
explanation: When no built-in role fits, a custom role with just those VM actions, scoped narrowly, is the least-privilege answer. Contributor at the VM scope is the tempting shortcut and grants far more than start and restart, including deletion.

prompt: Which two role systems can Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management govern with just-in-time elevation? (Choose two.)
choices: Microsoft Entra directory roles
Azure resource roles at scope
Key Vault vault access policy rules
Network security group rule sets
explanation: PIM manages Entra directory roles and Azure resource roles (plus PIM for Groups). NSG rules and Key Vault access policies are not PIM-governed.

prompt: Which two are true about the four fundamental built-in Azure roles? (Choose two.)
choices: Owner can grant access to other principals
User Access Administrator manages assignments only
Contributor can also grant access to other principals
Reader can modify the resource configuration
correctAnswers: Owner can grant access to other principals
User Access Administrator manages assignments only
explanation: Owner can grant access to others, and User Access Administrator can manage assignments without managing resources. Contributor is the trap: it manages resources fully whereas it cannot grant access, which is exactly the boundary that makes it safer than Owner.

prompt: Which two properties in a custom Azure role definition operate on the data plane? (Choose two.)
choices: The DataActions array
The NotDataActions array
The AssignableScopes array
The Actions array only
explanation: DataActions and NotDataActions govern data-plane operations. Actions and NotActions are the tempting pair because they look symmetrical, however they operate on the control plane — the two halves are deliberately separate.

prompt: Referring to requirement 1 (no standing Owner/Contributor rights; time-bound elevation gated by approval and MFA, max 4 hours), which configuration is correct?
choices: PIM eligibility with MFA, approval, 4-hour cap
A Conditional Access policy requiring MFA on the management plane
A custom role whose AssignableScopes expires after four hours
Assign Owner and rely on an Azure Policy audit
correctAnswers: PIM eligibility with MFA, approval, 4-hour cap
explanation: Only PIM delivers just-in-time, approval-gated, time-bound elevation with a maximum activation duration. Conditional Access controls sign-in, not standing assignments; AssignableScopes has no expiry.

prompt: Referring to requirement 2 (MFA on all Azure management sign-ins, but the break-glass account must never be locked out), which design is correct?
choices: MFA on the ARM API, break-glass excluded
A policy targeting Office 365 requiring MFA, with no exclusions
Enable per-VM just-in-time access for every administrator
Disable the break-glass account until an incident occurs
correctAnswers: MFA on the ARM API, break-glass excluded
explanation: Target the ARM control-plane resource, require MFA, and explicitly exclude the break-glass account so a policy fault can't lock everyone out.

prompt: Contoso wants an auditable record of every time an administrator elevates to a privileged role, including who approved it. Which feature provides this natively?
choices: PIM audit logs and access reviews
A Conditional Access report-only policy
A resource lock on the subscription
Storage account diagnostic logs
correctAnswers: PIM audit logs and access reviews
explanation: PIM audit logs record every activation, approval and assignment change, and access reviews recertify who still needs the role. A Conditional Access report-only policy is the tempting answer because it also produces logs, whereas it records sign-in evaluations rather than elevations.

prompt: Order the steps to activate a PIM-eligible Azure resource role, from the administrator's perspective.
reorderItems: Sign in to the Entra admin center
Go to Privileged Identity Management ▸ Azure resources ▸ My roles
Select 'Activate' next to the eligible role
Complete the required MFA, justification, and/or approval prompts
Use the role during the active, time-bound window
explanation: Activation runs from My roles, through the Activate action, then satisfying the configured gates, and finally using the role for its bounded window. Expecting the role to be usable straight from the assignment is the misconception that eligibility exists to prevent, whereas an active assignment would behave that way.

prompt: Order the steps to configure and safely roll out a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for the Azure management plane.
reorderItems: Browse to Conditional Access ▸ Policies ▸ New policy
Assign the target users/groups, excluding break-glass accounts
Under Target resources, select Windows Azure Service Management API
Under Grant, select Require multifactor authentication
Enable the policy in Report-only mode and review sign-in logs
Switch the policy from Report-only to On
explanation: Configure the assignment and grant controls, pilot in Report-only, then enforce. Enforcing before piloting is the ordering mistake, and it is not recoverable from inside the portal if the policy locks out the administrators.

prompt: Configure this simplified role-assignment screen so a contractor group can view resources in a resource group but cannot modify them or grant access to others.
explanation: Reader satisfies view-only with no modification and no ability to grant access, scoped as narrowly as the task allows. Contributor is the tempting default in this screen, whereas it would let the contractor change everything they can see.

prompt: Proposed solution: Assign every administrator the Contributor role directly at the subscription, and require MFA at every sign-in. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: This leaves a standing, permanent Contributor assignment with no approval gate or 4-hour limit — it does not meet the just-in-time requirement.

prompt: Proposed solution: Create a Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for the Azure management plane, and grant every administrator the Contributor role permanently. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: MFA on sign-in doesn't address the requirement for no standing privileged access, approval, or a 4-hour limit — the Contributor grant remains permanent.

prompt: Proposed solution: Make every administrator eligible for the required Azure roles via Privileged Identity Management, requiring MFA and approval at activation, with a 4-hour maximum activation duration. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
explanation: PIM eligibility with MFA, approval and a four-hour cap satisfies every part of the requirement, including the audit trail. Note the operational cost it accepts: administrators must now elevate before working, which is the behaviour change the requirement is asking for rather than a side effect.

prompt: Complete the Azure CLI command so that it grants user@contoso.com the Reader role on resource group RG1 and nowhere wider.
explanation: An assignment binds an existing role to a principal at a scope; a definition is the role itself, which is what makes `az role definition create` the tempting near-miss here — it would create a role rather than grant one. The scope must be the full resource ID: `/subscriptions/<subId>` grants Reader over every resource group in the subscription, and the two short forms are not scopes at all, so the command fails rather than over-granting.

prompt: Which PowerShell cmdlet assigns a built-in role to a user on a resource group?
choices: New-AzRoleAssignment
New-AzRoleDefinitionFile
Set-AzRoleAssignment
Add-AzADGroupMember
explanation: New-AzRoleAssignment creates the assignment. New-AzRoleDefinition creates a custom role definition; Set-AzRoleAssignment doesn't exist; Add-AzADGroupMember manages group membership.

prompt: You authored customRole.json with Actions and AssignableScopes. Complete the command that creates the custom role from that file.
explanation: A custom role is a role DEFINITION, so `az role assignment create` is the wrong half of the pair — it grants a role that must already exist. The `@` prefix is the Azure CLI convention meaning "read the value from this file": without it the CLI receives the literal string customRole.json rather than the JSON inside it, and rejects it as malformed even though the file is perfectly valid.

prompt: Complete the command so that it lists every role assignment effective on resource group RG1, including those inherited from the subscription.
explanation: Without `--include-inherited` the command lists only assignments made AT that scope, which is why an audit run this way reports a resource group as unprivileged while a subscription Owner has full control of it. `--all` is the tempting neighbour and does something different: it lists assignments across all scopes you can read rather than resolving inheritance onto one. `--recursive` is not a parameter of this command at all.

prompt: In a custom role's JSON, which snippet grants read on everything while denying nothing at the data plane?
choices: "Actions": ["*/read"], "DataActions": []
"NotActions": ["*/read"], "DataActions": ["*"]
"Actions": [], "NotDataActions": ["*/read"]
"AssignableScopes": ["*/read"]
explanation: */read under Actions grants control-plane read everywhere; an empty DataActions grants nothing at the data plane. NotActions/NotDataActions subtract, and AssignableScopes takes scopes, not operations.
